You have seen this chart. Everyone has.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(hpi, aes(m, idx)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f5c8a", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(peak), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey55") +
  annotate("label", x = peak, y = 130, hjust = 0, size = 3, fill = "white",
           label = "the peak — and the line every\nheadline was written about") +
  labs(title = "V1 · The chart everyone saw",
       subtitle = "THE LOGIC: this line is accurate. Nothing in this post disputes it. The question is what it is a footprint OF.",
       x = NULL, y = "House price index (2005 = 100)",
       caption = paste("HOW TO READ: national composite index; the decline from peak is the 'correction'.",
       "CONTEXT: an aggregate describes the market — it does not say on whom the change landed.",
       "DRAFT — SYNTHETIC series shaped on CREA/Teranet behaviour; production uses CREA MLS HPI + Teranet CSVs.", sep = "\n"))
```

The line fell, and a label arrived with it: *correction*. The label came with borrowed
knowledge — markets resetting, housing getting affordable, a bubble deflating. That is
the usual path: **data → borrowed label → assumed understanding.**

This post walks the other path: **data → which event generated this, and on whose ledger
does it act? → understanding.** The two paths end in different places.

## What a house price is, on a family's balance sheet

A purchase price is two things stacked: the family's down payment, and the bank's
mortgage. In Canada, a conventional purchase means at least 20% down; below that,
mortgage default insurance is legally required — and the **premium is paid by the
borrower**. <!-- ⚠ verify current CMHC thresholds & premium schedule before publication -->

So consider the simplest possible house: bought for 100, with 20 down and 80 borrowed.
Now let the index fall about 20% — roughly what the aggregate line above did.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
led <- data.frame(when = factor(rep(c("At purchase", "After a 20% decline"), each = 2),
                                levels = c("At purchase", "After a 20% decline")),
                  part = factor(rep(c("Owner's equity", "Bank's mortgage"), 2),
                                levels = c("Bank's mortgage", "Owner's equity")),
                  val  = c(20, 80, 0, 80))
ggplot(led, aes(when, val, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = .55) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Owner's equity" = "#a4770e", "Bank's mortgage" = "#9B958D"), name = NULL) +
  annotate("label", x = 2, y = 92, size = 3.2, fill = "white",
           label = "price: −20%\nbank's ledger: 0%\nowner's ledger: −100%") +
  labs(title = "V2 · One house, two ledgers",
       subtitle = "THE LOGIC: the same event has a different magnitude on each ledger it touches. Leverage is the multiplier.",
       x = NULL, y = "Value",
       caption = paste("HOW TO READ: the grey block is untouched; the amber block is gone. A 20% market event",
       "is a 100% household event at 20% down. CONTEXT: arithmetic — no dataset required, no dataset can soften it.", sep = "\n"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/v2-ledgers-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


Nothing controversial happened in that chart. It is the arithmetic every mortgage
contract already contains. It is also absent from essentially every rendering of V1.

## Whose event was it?

Apply the real index path to real purchase years, each at 20% down, and the single
"correction" separates into very different events:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cohorts <- data.frame(year = 2013:2025)
cohorts$entry <- sapply(cohorts$year, function(y) mean(hpi$idx[format(hpi$m, "%Y") == as.character(y)]))
now <- tail(hpi$idx, 1)
cohorts$equity_change <- pmax(-100, ((now - cohorts$entry) / (cohorts$entry * 0.20)) * 100)
ggplot(cohorts, aes(factor(year), equity_change,
                    fill = equity_change < 0)) +
  geom_col(width = .7, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#9B958D", "TRUE" = "#a4770e")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -100, linetype = "dotted", colour = "#7a1f1f") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.2, y = -92, size = 3, colour = "#7a1f1f",
           label = "−100% = the entire down payment") +
  labs(title = "V3 · The same correction, one event per purchase year",
       subtitle = "THE LOGIC: 'the market corrected' is one sentence. On household ledgers it is a dozen different events,\nfrom 'gave back some gains' to 'all of our savings'.",
       x = "Year the family bought (20% down)", y = "Change in the family's equity (%)",
       caption = paste("HOW TO READ: bars near zero barely noticed; deep amber bars lived a different event entirely.",
       "CONTEXT: the aggregate line (V1) contains all of these and reveals none of them.",
       "DRAFT — SYNTHETIC index; production computes this from CREA/Teranet monthly series.", sep = "\n"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/v3-cohorts-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


## The order in which losses arrive

This asymmetry is not an accident of arithmetic; it is a design, in three layers.
First loss: the owner's equity. Second: the default insurance that small-downpayment
borrowers themselves paid for. Third: in most provinces, mortgages are full recourse —
a shortfall can follow the borrower beyond the house.
<!-- ⚠ verify recourse rules by province (AB/SK differ) before publication -->
The bank's ledger sits behind all three. Described, not judged: the system is built so
that the people in the house absorb the event first.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lad <- data.frame(layer = factor(c("1 · Owner's equity", "2 · Borrower-paid insurance",
                                   "3 · Recourse on other assets", "4 · The bank"),
                  levels = rev(c("1 · Owner's equity", "2 · Borrower-paid insurance",
                                 "3 · Recourse on other assets", "4 · The bank"))),
                  x1 = c(0, 20, 32, 44), x2 = c(20, 32, 44, 100))
ggplot(lad) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = x1, xmax = x2, ymin = as.numeric(layer) - .35,
                ymax = as.numeric(layer) + .35),
            fill = c("#D6D3D1", "#9B958D", "#a4770e", "#a4770e")[4:1]) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = levels(lad$layer)) +
  labs(title = "V4 · Who absorbs a decline, in order",
       subtitle = "THE LOGIC: losses travel a designed sequence before reaching the lender's ledger.",
       x = "Depth of decline absorbed →", y = NULL,
       caption = "HOW TO READ: schematic, not to scale. CONTEXT: description of the contract structure, not an accusation of anyone.")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html/v4-ladder-1.png){width=864}
:::
:::


## Honesty about the way up

The same 5:1 leverage produced the gains of 2015–2022 — the mechanism has no
direction. Families who bought early rode the multiplier up before anyone rode it down.
This post describes a lens, not a villain.

## The clock that makes paper losses real

A Canadian mortgage renews roughly every five years. A family that never sells still
meets today's rates on a schedule — the unrealized event has an appointment with the
household's cash flow. <!-- ⚠ verify current BoC renewal-wave figures; V6 chart from
Bank of Canada Valet series to be added at build -->

## This was never about housing

Replace "national price index" with "company revenue," and "purchase-year cohorts"
with "customer segments," and reread V1 and V3. An aggregate can be perfectly accurate
while the event happens entirely inside its distribution — the same pattern as
[the Nokia case](#), where every KPI was green while the ground moved.

## What the data could not have told you

- Sometimes data alone is hard to place — *where* is it acting? **More data is not
  more understanding.** Ten more aggregate indicators would have made the borrowed
  label more confident, not more correct.
- You need to understand the **Event**, because the Event is what influences things;
  data is a tool that describes reality — and like any description, it may simply
  not be correct about what it is describing.
